result.summary: Pausanias finishes describing Titane's temples and rites, then travels the coast road toward Sicyon and its harbours. He enters Phliasia and relates its early traditions: the founder Aras, his children Aoris and Aræthyrea, and Phlias.

scenes.title: Titane: Athene and the winds
scenes.summary: At Titane stand a temple of Athene with an old wooden statue, and an altar of the winds where a priest performs nightly yearly rites.

scenes.title: Coast road toward Sicyon
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes a roofless temple of Hera, a temple of Poseidon, and the rivers Helisson and Sythas.

scenes.title: Introducing Phliasia
scenes.summary: Pausanias locates Phlius and argues the Phliasians were originally Argives, not Arcadians.

scenes.title: Aras and his children
scenes.summary: Aras founds Arantia; Asopus finds the river; Aoris and Aræthyrea rename the city, and their tombs receive libations.

scenes.title: The parentage of Phlias
scenes.summary: Pausanias rejects the Argive story of Phlias's descent and cites a poet to give his parents.

alias_notes.explanation: The poet quoted is the author of the Argonautica.

analysis.text: Pausanias combines travel description with local tradition, weighing rival accounts of origins and preferring evidence from poets such as Homer.
The winds rite and Medea's incantations show surviving local magical cult, while the Phliasian origin debate reflects Greek concern with ancestry and Dorian migration.

language_notes.text: Coronis was the mother of Asclepius by Apollo. Her statue is carried to Athene's temple in a ritual connected with the Asclepius cult at Titane.
Medea, the sorceress of Colchis, was famed for magic and charms, so her incantations suit a rite meant to calm violent winds.
"With neither statue nor roof" means the temple stood empty and open to the sky, a ruin or unfinished building.
Prœtus, son of Abas, was a legendary king of Argos and Tiryns, so this ruined temple is given a heroic founder.
The Catalogue of Ships in the Iliad lists the Arcadian contingent. Pausanias uses its omission of Phlius as evidence.
The return of the Heraclidae was the legendary Dorian invasion of the Peloponnese by Heracles' descendants, which changed the population of many cities.
Autochthon means 'sprung from the soil': a native whose people had always lived in the land, not immigrants.
Homer's Catalogue of Ships in the Iliad lists the contingents that sailed with Agamemnon to Ilium (Troy).
Libations are offerings of wine, milk or water poured out for gods or the dead.
The Rhodian poet is Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the Argonautica, the epic of the Argo's voyage.

context_notes.text: Winds were worshipped as powerful divine forces, especially by sailors and farmers, and were appeased with sacrifices.
A stade was about 600 Greek feet, roughly 180 metres, so forty stades is a little under five miles.
The Phliasians are the people of Phlius, a small city in the northeastern Peloponnese, whose early history Pausanias is recounting.
Ceres is the goddess of grain and harvest, the Roman name for the Greek Demeter; the rites honour her.
Dionysus is the god of wine, which fits Phlias being called wealthy through his father.

literary_notes.text: The secret rites and borrowed magic of Medea give the priest an eerie, half-magical character and make the winds seem like beings to be tamed.
Pausanias presents himself as a cautious reporter who gives local traditions but marks them as the Phliasians' own account.
The city's changed name is explained by a family death, a typical way Pausanias accounts for place names.
Pausanias speaks in the first person, weighing sources and rejecting the Argive tradition, which shows his critical, evidence-based method.
